clinicalPearls: Most often caused by extensive infarction of the ventral pons from basilar artery thrombosis, damaging the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts bilaterally
The patient is quadriplegic and anarthric but fully conscious and aware, with preserved cognition
Communication is typically possible only through vertical eye movements and blinking, which are mediated by spared midbrain structures
The reticular activating system is preserved, so the sleep-wake cycle and awareness remain intact, distinguishing it from coma
It must be actively distinguished from coma, persistent vegetative state, and severe Guillain-Barre syndrome
Other causes include central pontine myelinolysis, pontine haemorrhage, and rarely advanced neuromuscular disease
Early recognition allows a communication code to be established and appropriate supportive and rehabilitative care to begin
reference.pathophysiology: Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral interruption of the ventral pons, classically through basilar artery occlusion causing infarction of the basis pontis. The corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres are destroyed, abolishing voluntary movement of the limbs and lower cranial musculature and producing quadriplegia and anarthria. Crucially, the dorsal pontine tegmentum containing the reticular activating system is spared, so consciousness and cognition are retained, and supranuclear pathways for vertical gaze and blinking in the midbrain remain intact, providing the only avenue for voluntary responses. The disconnection of efferent motor output from an intact conscious brain gives the characteristic de-efferented state.
additionalDifferentials: Coma from bilateral hemispheric or brainstem dysfunction
Persistent vegetative or minimally conscious state
Severe Guillain-Barre syndrome with total paralysis
Deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade in critical care
additionalInvestigations: MRI with diffusion imaging demonstrating ventral pontine infarction
MR or CT angiography confirming basilar artery occlusion or stenosis
Electroencephalography showing preserved reactive background to confirm awareness
Assessment of vertical eye movements and blinking to establish communication and awareness
Electrolyte and osmolality review where central pontine myelinolysis is possible
Nerve conduction studies where a neuromuscular mimic is suspected
redFlags: Failure to recognise preserved awareness and misdiagnosis as coma or vegetative state
Evolving basilar thrombosis requiring urgent recanalisation consideration
Respiratory failure demanding airway protection and ventilatory support
Rapid osmotic shifts precipitating or worsening central pontine myelinolysis
reference.prognosis: Mortality is high in the acute basilar occlusion phase, and most survivors remain severely disabled, though some regain limited movement and many retain a meaningful quality of life with communication aids; recovery is generally slow and incomplete.
pitfalls: Mistaking a fully aware patient for being comatose and communicating inappropriately at the bedside
Overlooking preserved vertical gaze as the key sign of retained consciousness
Delaying recognition of basilar occlusion amenable to intervention
Correcting hyponatraemia too rapidly and inducing osmotic demyelination
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying basilar artery occlusion acutely with thrombolysis and/or mechanical thrombectomy when the patient presents within window
Provide neurocritical care with airway protection, ventilatory support and management of the acute stroke
Establish a reliable communication channel using preserved vertical eye movements and blinking, with eye-tracking and other assistive technology
Deliver comprehensive supportive care: enteral feeding via gastrostomy, tracheostomy, pressure-area and eye care, and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis
Prevent and treat complications such as aspiration pneumonia, contractures, spasticity and autonomic instability
Institute secondary stroke prevention with antithrombotic therapy and vascular risk-factor control, or correct the specific cause such as cautious sodium correction in central pontine myelinolysis
Provide intensive multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and communication therapy
Offer psychological support, honest prognostic discussion, goals-of-care planning and family support
